label: Japan

parties.name: Nippon Ishin no Kai (Japan Restoration Party)

governmentText.confidence_supply: {lead} governs with outside support from {partner} ({seats} seats).
governmentText.minority: {party} forms a minority government on {seats} seats and has to bargain for every vote in the House.
governmentText.hung: No combination reaches a majority. {largest} is the largest party, and the talks begin.

goalHint: Reach {majority} of {total} seats, alone or with a partner. Each region is a regional list block: its seats are its single-member districts plus its list seats, so the party that wins the block takes most of them, and a swing moves more seats than a pure list system would.

issues.name: Prices, wages & the yen
issues.blurb: Deflation, then inflation: stagnant pay, a swinging yen and the cost of everyday goods.

issues.name: Pensions & social security
issues.blurb: A shrinking workforce paying for the oldest population in the world.

issues.name: Consumption tax
issues.blurb: The 5, 8 and 10 percent rates, and whether to raise it again to pay for social security.

issues.name: Security & the constitution
issues.blurb: Article 9, the American bases in Okinawa, North Korea and a rising China.

issues.name: Nuclear power & energy
issues.blurb: Restarting reactors after Fukushima, or phasing them out.

issues.name: Politics & money
issues.blurb: Donations, factions, slush funds and who answers for them.

issues.name: Disaster reconstruction
issues.blurb: Tohoku after the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, and the next one to prepare for.

issues.name: Child support & the birth rate
issues.blurb: Allowances, free schooling and childcare in a country with too few children.

issues.name: COVID-19 response
issues.blurb: States of emergency, vaccines and the Olympic summer.

issues.name: Trade & farming
issues.blurb: The TPP, rice protection and what open markets do to the countryside.

2009.label: 2009 · Hatoyama v. Aso
2009.tagline: August 2009. Fifty-four years of near-unbroken LDP rule are on the line. Aso has run out of calendar, a third of his caucus wants him gone, and Hatoyama's Democrats promise child allowances and a change of government. Win the first real handover of power, or stop it.

events.headline: The Tokyo assembly election leaves the LDP without its place as the largest party for the first time since 1965, and {party} is rattled
Aso dissolves the House on 21 July as a third of his own caucus signs a petition for him to go, and {party} fights the campaign divided
The Democratic manifesto promises 26,000 yen a month per child, free expressways and no sales tax rise for four years, and {party} gets a hearing
Yoshimi Watanabe launches Your Party, a civil service reform ticket for voters tired of both big parties, and {party} is on the ballot within weeks
Aso and the LDP spend the official campaign asking where the Democrats will find the money, and {party} hopes older voters listen
The big papers report the Democrats are on course for more than 300 seats, and {party} gets a bandwagon on top of its lead
The lost pension records come up at every rally, and {party} owns the anger of voters whose pension records the state lost
Unemployment hits a postwar record, and {party} takes the blame for the downturn
Ozawa, who resigned the leadership over a donation scandal, is still the party's election strategist, and {party} wobbles at the mention of his name
Soka Gakkai members work the phone banks in the marginal seats, and {party} holds its core
Hatoyama tells voters in Okinawa the Futenma base should move out of the prefecture, a promise that will be hard to keep, and {party} wins friends on the islands

issues.name: Pension records
issues.blurb: Some 50 million pension records the state could not match, and the new health scheme for over-75s.

issues.name: Recession and jobs
issues.blurb: The deepest postwar slump after the Lehman shock, temp worker layoffs and unemployment at 5.7 percent.

issues.name: Child allowance
issues.blurb: The Democrats' 26,000 yen a month per child, against the LDP's offer of free preschool.

issues.name: Bureaucrats and waste
issues.blurb: Retired officials parachuting into public bodies, wasteful spending and Ozawa's aide's donation case.

issues.name: Consumption tax
issues.blurb: Aso's plan to raise it once the economy recovered, against the Democrats' four-year freeze.

issues.name: North Korea and bases
issues.blurb: North Korea's May nuclear test and Hatoyama's call to move Futenma out of Okinawa.

issues.name: Farm trade
issues.blurb: The Democrats' US free trade pledge, softened after farm protests, and income support for farmers.

2012.label: 2012 · Abe v. Noda
2012.tagline: December 2012. Noda has promised to dissolve the House after three years of Democratic government, a third pole is forming overnight, and Abe wants his old job back. The anti-Democratic vote has several places to go, and the LDP does not need to be loved.

events.headline: Noda tells Abe in a televised debate he will dissolve the House within days. Three years of Democratic government end, and {party} limps into the campaign
Hashimoto's Restoration Party and Ishihara's Sunrise Party merge into one third force, and {party} jumps in the polls
Governor Kada launches the Tomorrow Party with Ozawa's followers behind her and a promise to end nuclear power, and {party} becomes the new home for anti-nuclear voters
The Sasago Tunnel ceiling collapse kills nine and puts ageing infrastructure on the front page, and {party} promises national resilience
North Korea fires a long-range rocket over Okinawa four days before the vote, and {party}'s tough line on security sounds like common sense
Ishihara and Hashimoto differ in public on nuclear power and the trade deal, and {party} looks less like a new force and more like a merger of two
Abe's call for unlimited easing sends the yen down and stocks up, and {party} looks like the market's pick
The consumption tax law Noda passed with the LDP and Komeito is the 2009 manifesto turned inside out, and {party} pays the price
After the nationalisation of the Senkaku Islands and the protests in China, the LDP's hard line sounds like leadership, and {party} gains
Anti-nuclear crowds outside the prime minister's office every Friday put the issue on every front page, and {party} owns the argument on the left
Your Party turns down a merger with the Restoration Party and keeps its own line, and {party} wins respect from civil service reformers

issues.name: Deflation and the yen
issues.blurb: Years of falling prices, a yen near 80 to the dollar and Abe's call for 2 percent inflation.

issues.name: Nuclear power
issues.blurb: Reactors idle after Fukushima, the Oi restart in July and pledges to phase out nuclear in the 2030s.

issues.name: Consumption tax rise
issues.blurb: The August law to double the tax to 10 percent by 2015, which the 2009 manifesto had ruled out.

issues.name: Senkaku and China
issues.blurb: The September purchase of the Senkaku Islands, the protests in China and the row over Takeshima.

issues.name: Tohoku reconstruction
issues.blurb: Rebuilding after the 2011 tsunami, the Fukushima evacuees and reconstruction money spent elsewhere.

issues.name: TPP
issues.blurb: Whether to join the Trans-Pacific Partnership talks, which farm groups and many LDP members opposed.

2014.label: 2014 · Abe v. Kaieda
2014.tagline: December 2014. Japan has slipped into recession, Abe has put off the sales tax rise and called an election to ask whether Abenomics is working. The Democrats are weak, the Communists see a gap, and nobody expects a crowd at the polls.

events.headline: The economy shrinks again in the summer quarter and Japan is back in recession, and {party} is blamed for the sales tax rise that did it
Abe delays the sales tax rise by eighteen months and dissolves the House to ask voters whether Abenomics is right, and {party} frames it as a choice with no alternative
Okinawa had just elected a governor who opposes the Futenma base move, and {party} takes the base question to the mainland
Real wages have fallen for more than a year while prices rise, and the opposition leader Kaieda calls Abenomics a failure for ordinary families. {party} finally has a message
The State Secrets Act takes effect in the middle of the campaign, and {party}, which opposed it most loudly, picks up the protest vote
Heavy snow on the Sea of Japan coast and in Hokkaido keeps voters home on polling day, and the organised vote of {party} turns out anyway
The Bank of Japan's surprise easing and a weak yen lift the Nikkei to a seven-year high, and {party} points at the stock screens
The October resignations of two women ministers over funds and handout fans still hang over the cabinet, and {party} has to keep explaining
Komeito pushes a lower sales tax rate on food as the price of its support, and {party} claims credit with household budgets
Innovation, a party formed only three months earlier, gets little airtime outside Kansai, and {party} struggles to look like a national force
With the opposition parties running against each other in most districts, {party} struggles to look like the alternative

issues.name: Abenomics
issues.blurb: A recession after April's tax rise, a weaker yen and stocks at a seven-year high.

issues.name: Tax rise delay
issues.blurb: Abe's delay of the second rise, from 8 to 10 percent, by eighteen months to April 2017.

issues.name: Collective self-defence
issues.blurb: The July cabinet decision reinterpreting Article 9, and the State Secrets Act taking effect.

issues.name: Pensions and care
issues.blurb: The pension fund's October shift into shares, and the elderly care costs the tax rise was meant to fund.

issues.name: Nuclear restarts
issues.blurb: The Sendai reactors in Kagoshima cleared to restart, with every reactor in Japan offline since 2013.

issues.name: TPP and farming
issues.blurb: Talks on the Trans-Pacific Partnership and protection for rice, beef and dairy.

issues.name: Okinawa bases
issues.blurb: Onaga's November win for governor of Okinawa on opposition to moving Futenma to Henoko.

2017.label: 2017 · Abe v. Koike
2017.tagline: September 2017. Abe calls a snap election to catch a divided opposition, and Governor Koike launches a rival party the same evening. The Democrats split within days, North Korea is firing missiles overhead, and a two-thirds majority is on the table.

events.headline: Koike launches the Party of Hope on the evening Abe calls the election, and {party} leaps up the polls
Koike says she will 'exclude' the liberals from the Democrats who want to join her, and {party} loses its shine overnight
Edano launches the Constitutional Democratic Party for the liberals left out in the cold, and {party} gets a groundswell of sympathy
Critics say Abe called the election to avoid questions about the Moritomo and Kake school scandals, and {party} has to answer them as the official campaign opens
Polls show the ruling bloc heading for a landslide against an opposition split three ways, and {party} looks like the only safe choice
Typhoon Lan brings wind and rain on polling day. Organised voters turn out and floating voters stay home, and {party} gains from the weather
Missiles over Hokkaido and a nuclear test have the sirens going, and {party}'s tough line on North Korea sounds like common sense
Abe promises to spend the sales tax rise on free early education and childcare, and {party} steals the opposition's best issue
Ishin agrees to stay out of Hope's way in Tokyo and Osaka, and {party} rides along on Koike's publicity
The Communists withdraw from dozens of districts to help Edano, and {party} gets less airtime and a smaller slate
Hope promises to freeze the sales tax rise and phase out nuclear power by 2030, but nobody can say what it adds up to, and {party} gets questions it cannot answer

issues.name: North Korea
issues.blurb: Missiles fired over Hokkaido in August and September, and the North's sixth nuclear test.

issues.name: Consumption tax rise
issues.blurb: Whether the 2019 rise to 10 percent goes ahead, and Abe's plan to spend part of it on education.

issues.name: Abenomics
issues.blurb: Record company profits and near full employment, against real wages that barely rose.

issues.name: Free education
issues.blurb: Abe's pledge of free preschool and childcare, and the opposition's own offers for families.

issues.name: Moritomo and Kake
issues.blurb: A discounted land sale to a school operator and a vet school approved for a friend of Abe.

issues.name: Revising Article 9
issues.blurb: Abe's May proposal to write the Self-Defense Forces into Article 9 by 2020.

issues.name: Nuclear phase-out
issues.blurb: Hope's pledge of zero nuclear power by 2030, the CDP's own exit plan and the restarts under way.

2021.label: 2021 · Kishida v. Edano
2021.tagline: October 2021. Suga is gone after a pandemic summer, Kishida is ten days into the job, and the opposition has agreed to field one candidate against the LDP in most districts. Win a majority on a fresh face, or break the LDP's hold.

events.headline: Kishida beats three rivals for the LDP leadership and becomes prime minister on 4 October, and the party looks like {party} with a fresh face
Edano's party, the Communists, the Social Democrats and Reiwa agree to stand one candidate per district and a common platform, and {party} finally looks like an alternative
Ishin promises a basic income, free education written into the constitution and Osaka-style reform, and {party} breaks out of its home base
Kishida's leadership promise of a higher tax on financial income quietly disappears from the manifesto, and {party} looks less new than advertised
The fifth wave has collapsed and the state of emergency is a memory, and voters give the incumbent {party} the benefit of the doubt
The LDP and the conservative papers brand the opposition pact a 'Communist coalition', and swing voters flinch away from {party}
The opposition's promise to cut the consumption tax from 10 to 5 percent for a time gets a hearing, and {party} gains among households squeezed by the pandemic
Komeito's promise of 100,000 yen for every child under 18 is the loudest handout of the campaign, and {party} holds its base
Osaka's covid death toll, the highest in Japan in the spring wave, is thrown at Ishin's record in government, and {party} loses ground
Taro Yamamoto drops his Tokyo district bid to help the opposition pact and runs on the list, and {party} gets a modest lift
Tamaki's smaller party insists on its own line, neither the LDP's nor the pact's, and {party} wins over voters tired of both camps

issues.name: COVID-19 response
issues.blurb: The fifth wave that overwhelmed hospitals in August, the vaccine rollout and the Olympic summer.

issues.name: Wages and 'new capitalism'
issues.blurb: Kishida's pledge to share the gains of growth with workers, and cash support for pandemic losses.

issues.name: China and defence
issues.blurb: Pressure on Taiwan, North Korean missiles and an LDP pledge with 2 percent of GDP for defence in mind.

issues.name: Politics and money
issues.blurb: Abe's cherry blossom dinners, the Moritomo files and a former justice minister's vote-buying conviction.

issues.name: Cash for children
issues.blurb: Komeito's 100,000 yen for every child under 18, and wider handouts promised by most parties.

issues.name: Consumption tax cut
issues.blurb: Opposition calls to cut the 10 percent tax to 5 percent for a time.

issues.name: Energy and climate
issues.blurb: Reactor restarts and how to reach the 2050 carbon neutrality goal Suga set in 2020.

2024.label: 2024 · Ishiba v. Noda
2024.tagline: October 2024. Ishiba called the election eight days after becoming prime minister, with the slush fund scandal still open and prices still rising. The LDP and Komeito could lose their majority for the first time since 2009. Take the government from them, or hold on with a weaker hand.

events.headline: Ishiba drops his pledge to debate in the Diet first and calls an election eight days into the job, and critics say {party} is putting itself ahead of the country
The LDP withdraws its endorsement from twelve members caught up in the slush fund scandal, and the party that promised to clean up still looks like {party}
Noda runs against the slush fund and for a change of government, and {party} climbs for the first time in years
Tamaki's pitch to lift the 1.03 million yen income wall and raise take-home pay goes viral among young workers, and {party} pulls ahead of its poll numbers
The Communist daily reveals that the LDP sent 20 million yen to the branches of the candidates it refused to endorse, and {party} cannot talk its way out of it
Ishiba reminds voters of the 'nightmare' of the last Democratic government, and {party} gets a late hearing from nervous conservatives
Sanseito fills halls built on YouTube clips and anger at the establishment, and {party} wins over voters who never trusted a party before
Reiwa's pledge to scrap the consumption tax and hand out cash finds an audience among the squeezed, and {party} gains on the left
Ishin's cooperation with the LDP on the political funds law is questioned at home, and {party} loses its edge as the reform party
Naoki Hyakuta's new Conservative Party packs rallies with an online following, and {party} becomes a protest option on the right
Noda courts moderate conservatives with a middle-of-the-road security line, the left of the party and the Communists grumble, and {party} looks less like a united alternative
Ishiba's pitch for rural revival and the LDP's branch network hold the countryside, and {party} keeps its provincial base
Komeito's new leader Keiichi Ishii is in a tight fight for his own Saitama seat a month after taking the job, and {party} spends its energy defending him

issues.name: Slush fund scandal
issues.blurb: Faction fundraising kickbacks kept off the books, and the twelve members the LDP refused to endorse.

issues.name: Prices and take-home pay
issues.blurb: Rice and food prices rising faster than wages, and the 1.03 million yen income wall.

issues.name: Children and the birth rate
issues.blurb: Kishida's 3.6 trillion yen plan for children and the new support levy added to health insurance.

issues.name: Defence spending
issues.blurb: Doubling defence spending to 2 percent of GDP by 2027, and how to pay for it.

issues.name: Social security
issues.blurb: Pensions for an ageing population and the December switch from paper health cards to My Number cards.

issues.name: Noto recovery
issues.blurb: Rebuilding on the Noto peninsula after the New Year's Day earthquake and the September floods.

2026.label: 2026 · Takaichi v. Noda
2026.tagline: February 2026. Sanae Takaichi, Japan's first woman prime minister, has governed for three months in coalition with Ishin, after Komeito walked out of the old LDP coalition. She dissolves the House to ask for a mandate of her own in the shortest campaign since the war. Against her, the Constitutional Democrats and Komeito have merged into the Centrist Reform Alliance.

events.headline: Takaichi announces on 19 January that she will dissolve the House at the opening of the Diet, turning the vote into a referendum on her leadership and the coalition with Ishin, and {party} rides her approval ratings

The House is dissolved on 23 January. The Constitutional Democrats and Komeito fight it as one party, the Centrist Reform Alliance, with Komeito on the lists only, and old voters of both have to find {party} on the ballot
Sixteen days from dissolution to polling day, the shortest campaign since the war, and critics say {party} called the vote to avoid a debate
The row with Beijing over Takaichi's November remarks on Taiwan, with Chinese tourists told to stay away, keeps security at the top of the news, and {party} gains
Ishin campaigns on the cut in the number of Diet seats it made the price of joining the coalition, and {party} holds Osaka
Tamaki campaigns on take-home pay and the higher tax-free income threshold his party won from the government, and {party} keeps its young voters
Sanseito carries its 'Japanese First' message on foreign residents from its 2025 upper house breakthrough into the lower house, and {party} climbs
Takahiro Anno's Team Mirai, a young party of engineers, campaigns on technology and open government and draws crowds of city voters, and {party} rises

issues.name: Prices and take-home pay
issues.blurb: Rice and food prices outpacing pay, a weak yen and the higher tax-free income threshold.

issues.name: China and defence
issues.blurb: Beijing's anger at Takaichi's November remarks on a Taiwan emergency, and faster defence spending.

issues.name: Consumption tax on food
issues.blurb: Rival pledges to cut the 8 percent consumption tax on food, and how to pay for it.

issues.name: Foreign residents
issues.blurb: Rules for foreign residents, tourists and land purchases, pushed up the agenda by Sanseito's 2025 gains.

issues.name: Social insurance
issues.blurb: Pension levels and the social insurance premiums taken out of workers' pay.

issues.name: Politics and money
issues.blurb: Komeito's exit from the coalition over the slush funds, and limits on corporate donations.

issues.name: Cutting Diet seats
issues.blurb: Ishin's price for backing Takaichi: a cut of about a tenth in the number of lower house seats.

events.headline: A weak GDP print leads the evening news, and the government's economic record is questioned. {party} takes the hit
Another round of price rises at the supermarket and the pump puts the cost of living on the front page, and voters look to {party}
{party}'s leader wins the Japan National Press Club debate and the clip runs all night
A candidate's careless remark goes viral, and {party} spends the day apologising
A row over candidate selection spills into the papers, and {party} looks divided
Farm co-ops, trade associations and unions line up behind {party}
A street speech goes viral online and {party} wins a crowd of first-time voters
A tour of provincial towns wins {party} friendly local coverage
A typhoon and an earthquake test the government, and a calm, visible response helps {party}
A political funds report row hits the headlines and {party} has to explain it
NHK offers {party} a head-to-head debate slot
events.prompt: A prime-time leaders' debate is on the table. How do you play it?

choices.text: Accept and go on the attack
choices.resultText: You land blows and take a few. The overnight polls twitch your way.
A steady, on-message night. No gaffes, no fireworks.
You skip the studio lights. The press calls it a snub.

events.headline: Every interview asks {party} the same question: who would you govern with?
events.prompt: Voters want to know your coalition partners. What do you say?

choices.text: Name your partners and campaign as a bloc
choices.resultText: Clarity reassures your side. The other side calls it a stitch-up.
Nobody is ruled out, and nobody is quite reassured.

choices.text: Say you will govern alone or not at all
choices.resultText: A bold line. It sharpens the contrast with your rival.

events.headline: {party}'s policy chiefs are split on the headline pledge
events.prompt: The manifesto goes to the printers on Friday. Which way do you push?

choices.text: Go bold with a defining, costly pledge
choices.resultText: The base roars. The Finance Ministry starts sharpening pencils.

choices.text: Play it safe: no hostages to fortune
Make it a contrast with the rival's costings
choices.resultText: You define them more than yourself, and it lands.
